records.bodyText:
Portugal is drawing a line in the water. 
With gigantic new data centers planned across the country, Portugal says that under laws due next year they will have to run on renewable power, go through a full environmental review, and use cooling that does not rely on fresh water.
That matters. A single large data center can use millions of litres of water a day just to keep its machines cool, and in many places that water comes from the same rivers and reservoirs that families and farmers depend on. Southern Europe already knows what drought feels like.
Neighbouring Spain is moving too, planning to require large data centers to get 80% of their power from clean sources.
Technology can be built responsibly. It just has to be asked.

records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
Landscape standards in wind farm development
Can wind farm objectors rely on the professionalism of landscape architects working for developers?
Can they trust the Landscape Institute to uphold professional standards?
Not in my experience
After two years of trying privately to have my complaint given serious consideration by the Landscape Institute, I have written an open letter to its Trustees.
The summary below sets out the main points of that letter. I believe these could be relevant to others in a similar position.
Conclusions from my experience:
1. The Institute is not serious in investigating complaints
My complaint has been repeatedly dismissed, but I remain confident in my case.
I was therefore unsurprised when subject access disclosures revealed that the Institute had described my complaint as “Hugely Controversial” and suggested that “someone should talk to (me)”. Despite that suggestion, no one contacted me.
2. The subject of my complaint is probably endemic across the Wind Farm Industry
Why did someone within the Institute describe my complaint as “hugely controversial”?
An offer to provide a statement confirming the reviewer’s independence was withdrawn after I asked whether the reviewer was involved with any wind industry bodies.
3. The Review of my complaint was a whitewash
The review did not address some of the points I raised and misinterpreted the Institute’s own guidance on others.
Assuming the reviewer was appropriately selected from within the Institute’s leadership, this raises serious questions about the review’s conclusions. I believe that upholding my complaint could have wider implications for the wind farm and renewable energy industry.
4. The Institute’s Professional Code of Practice does not require members to follow its technical guidance notes
The Institute publishes many technical guidance notes. I find it difficult to understand why its Code of Practice—with 11 rules and 17 pages of explanation—does not explicitly require members to follow that guidance.
5. Landscape professionals are not held accountable for acting independently and consulting a cross section of the affected community.
In my experience, the Institute pays only lip service to its stated aim of “uphold(ing)……… competence and conduct of those who practice Landscape Architecture as a profession.”
Guidance acknowledges the professional’s involvement in a scheme while requiring an independent stance: “Landscape professionals are likely to be closely involved in the development of the scheme and its design……In carrying out an LVIA the Landscape professional must always take an independent stance…..”
The Code of Practice also calls for engagement with a range of community perspectives: “Landscape professionals should actively seek out a diversity of viewpoints in any engagement or consultation relating to landscape work. This includes ensuring a cross section of the affected community is consulted and that representatives of relevant communities are engaged.”
From my close involvement with a development, I have seen no evidence that the Institute member engaged with anyone other than their client and the client’s advisers.
6. The Institute’s published complaints guidance aims to prevent scrutiny of planning matters
The guidance states that the Institute cannot investigate certain matters, including:
· “An issue which relates to a current planning application or appeal”
· “Any matter that took place more than 6 months ago.”
In my view, these two restrictions conflict in the context of the planning process.
A full copy of the open letter can be found at: https://scotlandagainstspin.org/.../open-letter-to.../...
SCOTLANDAGAINSTSPIN.ORG Open letter to the Trustees of the Landscape Institute

F/V Mistress - USCG Document ECF No.14-7 Requiring Reopening Investigation
Why aren't they reopening the investigation?
Concerns Over Industry Ties: Critics have pointed to connections between retired regulatory personnel and both the oil transportation barges and offshore wind industry, noting past transitions of Coast Guard officials to roles with maritime interests. If a Coast Guard officer moves directly from a role where they inspected or regulated a specific oil barge or offshore wind company to a role with that company, it can create a perception of bias.
98,000 gallons of No. 6 heavy fuel oil into Buzzards Bay
The crew and captain involved in the 2003 Bouchard Barge No. 120 oil spill were not tested for drugs or alcohol until 18 hours after the accident occurred. In Buzzards Bay, during a standard small recreational safety check—like verifying life jackets or flares—if the operator shows any signs of impairment, a Coast Guard boarding team will immediately transition the encounter into a BUI investigation and conduct alcohol testing.
F/V Mistress lack of reopening an investigation over two months:
In the context of federal maritime investigations, ECF No. 14-7 refers to the January 2, 2020, U.S. Coast Guard (USCG) Investigative Determination regarding the sinking of the fishing vessel F/V Mistress. The final page of that report explicitly states that the case was closed "with the understanding the case would be re-opened pending receipt of information sufficient to determine the apparent cause of the MISTRESS disappearance."
In a 2022 U.S. District Court lawsuit in Rhode Island, a 2020 Coast Guard document (ECF No. 14-7). Exhibit 7, Docket Number 14, is 29 pages. On page 29, Coast Guard Headquarters closed the case with the understanding that it would be reopened pending receipt of information sufficient to determine the disappearance of the F/V Mistress.
The F/V Mistress sank on January 1, 2019. The Coast Guard considered the trawler lost. Green Oceans found it in August next to Block Island turbine #1.
.
Green Oceans sent the Coast Guard the information over two months ago. Physical evidence now exists, including sonar imagery, photographs, and potentially human remains.
.
The Administrative Procedure Act (APA) governs how the U.S. Coast Guard—as a federal agency—makes regulations, conducts formal hearings, and handles public accountability
Under the APA, federal agencies cannot simply sit on mandatory duties or formal commitments indefinitely. Failure to Act: Section 706(1) grants federal courts the authority to "compel agency action unlawfully withheld or unreasonably delayed."

records.title: Scottish Electricity Generating Stations
records.bodyText:
The Berwick Bank Wind Farm is a massive proposed offshore wind energy project in the outer Firth of Forth in the North Sea, developed by SSE Renewables.
Key Project Details
• Capacity: Up to 4.1 GW of installed capacity, making it one of the largest offshore wind developments in the world.
• Power Generation: Capable of generating enough clean energy to power over 6 million homes (more than twice all Scottish households).
• Project Phases: Split into three phases (including Berwick Bank A, B, and C), with phase B having secured a Contract for Difference (CfD) in January 2026.
• Grid Connections: Connected to the national transmission network at Branxton in East Lothian (consented by the Scottish Government in July 2025) and via the Cambois Connection near Blyth in Northumberland (which received marine licence approval in November 2026).
• Timeline: Final Investment Decision (FID) is expected around 2027–2028, with offshore construction and first power targeted toward 2028.
• Economic Impact: Projected to generate up to £8.3 billion for the UK economy and create over 9,000 UK-based jobs (around 4,650 in Scotland) at peak construction.
SSE completed Berwick Bank C connection permits with the maritime authorization allowing the third phase of the Berwick Bank wind farm to be connected to the national grid via HVDC cables.
SSE Renewables has obtained maritime authorization to develop the electrical infrastructure of Berwick Bank C, the third phase of its 4.1 GW offshore wind project in the UK has been granted permission by the Marine Management Organisation (MMO) to complete the regulatory procedures necessary to connect this phase to the national transmission grid.
The authorization belongs to Cambois Connection, the system that will transport the electricity generated at the wind farm to Northumberland, in northeast England.
Berwick Bank C will have an HVDC connection of up to 1.8 GW
The project envisions the installation of up to four high-voltage direct current submarine cables (HVDC), with a combined transmission capacity of up to 1,8 GW. These cables will carry electricity from Berwick Bank C to Cambois, near Blyth, where the connection to the national grid will be established.
HVDC technology is particularly well-suited for transporting large volumes of electricity over long distances, as it reduces transmission losses. Its application in offshore wind farms facilitates the integration of energy generated at sea with onshore electrical systems.
On land, the infrastructure will include the cable landing point, a converter station, and the facilities necessary to incorporate the electricity into the national grid.The license completes the permissions of Cambois Connection
The MMO authorization culminates a regulatory process that has progressed in stages over the past few years. In November 2024, Northumberland County Council approved the onshore transmission facilities. Subsequently, in July 2025, the Scottish Government authorized the development of the Berwick Bank wind farm in Scottish waters, along with the planned evacuation cables to Branxton in East Lothian.
With this latest decision, the project completes the authorizations for its electrical infrastructure, organized around two connection points, the first being in Branxton and the second one is in Blyth.
However, obtaining the permits does not imply the immediate start of construction, investments, contracting of the work, and execution schedules must progress according to the planning of each phase.@
Located in the outer Firth of Forth, approximately 38km east of the Scottish coast, Berwick Bank is among a list offshore wind developments planned across the country.
The offshore wind project is divided into three phases which, once completed, would total 4.1 GW of installed capacity, according to the project’s estimates, that power would allow for the annual generation of enough electricity to cover the equivalent consumption of more than six million homes.
Given its scale, the project represents a significant addition of renewable capacity to the @electricity system. However, its implementation will depend on investment decisions, trade agreements, and the construction of generation and transmission infrastructure. Li
While the third phase connection progresses, SSE Renewables is also preparing the next steps to Berwick Bank B, which will have a planned capacity of 1.4 GW.
In January 2026, this phase secured a 20-year contract for difference (CfD) during the UK’s seventh allocation round, known as Allocation Round 7. This mechanism provides a revenue framework for the electricity the project will generate and supports its financial development.
In the UK's Contracts for Difference (CfD) Allocation Round 7 (AR7), announced in January 2026, the strike prices for offshore wind were awarded at:
Fixed-Bottom Offshore Wind (Scotland): £89.49/MWh (in 2024 prices) 
Key Details from AR7
• Administrative Strike Price Cap: Set at £113/MWh for standard offshore wind prior to the auction.
• Contract Duration: Contracts awarded under AR7 run for an extended 20-year term (increased from previous 15-year terms). 
• Capacity Procured: A record total of around 8.4 GW of offshore wind capacity was secured across fixed-bottom and floating projects.
With this contract, SSE plans to reach the final investment decision in 2027, the company also selected Seaway7 as preferred supplier for the engineering, supply, construction and installation of the foundations and interconnecting cables for this phase.
As for Berwick Bank A and C, both phases could participate in future rounds of contract for difference allocation. For now, the authorization of Cambois Connection represents progress for Berwick Bank C, as it resolves an essential regulatory requirement before developing its electrical connection infrastructure.
I think this project should be renamed as East of the Kingdom of Fife Energy Hub, just to highlight where it’s actually located.— at The Forth Estuary.

records.bodyText:
Scottish AI data centre developers ditch renewables to rely fully on National Grid
DEVELOPERS of a hyperscale AI data centre near Glasgow have admitted it will fully rely on the National Grid despite previously claiming the facility would be powered by renewable energy.
The National revealed in September that DataVita submitted proposals for a 120MW “green data centre” in Chapelhall, North Lanarkshire, south of the junction between Lancaster Avenue and Bellside Road.
Developers originally claimed the AI facility would draw up to 1GW directly from dedicated green energy sources including wind, solar, and battery storage, which would be “delivered through private wire connections directly linked to the data centre”.
However, DataVita has since U-turned on its previous announcement, as it told The Guardian its complex will instead rely entirely on the National Grid.
A DataVita spokesperson told the newspaper it had not misrepresented its intention to supply renewables to the site earlier this year, claiming their “commitment to renewable energy is unchanged”.
The spokesperson added: “Our datacentres are being designed to be grid served … Our grid supply will be through a renewable power purchase agreement.”
Kat Jones, the director of Action to Protect Rural Scotland, said DataVita’s change in power plans was “emblematic of the hyperbolic claims being made by data centre developers in Scotland”.
She said: “Hyperscale AI datacentres simply cannot run on renewable power alone, they absolutely need a highly reliable source of grid power.”
Adding: “It is not surprising that the goalposts have now changed.”
It comes after it was revealed in September there had been fears from locals and campaign groups over DataVita’s backup engine plans for the North Lanarkshire site.
The generators would expand the site’s power capacity when peak customer demand coincided with air temperatures above 21C. Up to 32 of the total 48 generators could start operating in “load support mode” to help cool computing equipment, planning documents show.
Jen Thompson, who lives 50m from the proposed site, said the potential air pollution and noise were a “massive worry” for her four children.
At the time, the Scottish Greens called for a definition of a “green data centre” to “exclude the use of polluting diesel generators”.
DataVita already runs another data centre in Chapelhall – the DV1 site – which, at a capacity of 24MW, makes it the largest data centre in Scotland currently in operation.
The DV1 data centre provides server networks to nearby businesses, with expansion work planned to increase its capacity to around 40MW.
The new site, which is called DV4, is classed as a "hyperscale" data centre due to the large number of megawatts required to run it.
The latest plans would fall inside Scotland's first AI Growth Zone, which was announced would be in Lanarkshire earlier this year

Nick MacKinnon has a great blog out which for some reason I haven't drawn to your attention.
Things are not going well for CEP and Al-Gihaz. Deep Stoat is supplying us with excellent inside information, and Al-Gihaz and CEP are being bombarded with legal letters...
What we liked best [about the article in the Telegraph] (and my father-in-law noticed its significance) was that the article concluded with this sentence:
“Al Gihaz Holding was contacted for comment.”
It was good that the Telegraph contacted Mustapha Hajjar in Riyadh, an example of the once-vivid phrase: “Don’t ask the monkey; speak to the organ-grinder.” Hajjar cannot expect his comedy subsidiary to provide much protection now. The WTRG bog burst letter will cost him £100,000 just for the first reply, because somebody at Pinsent Masons [CEP's very expensive London lawyers]has to get an understanding of thixotropic peat at least as good as Haworth with Stanbury Parish Council’s. The itemised bill will include “Purchase of two copies of Charlotte Brontë at the Anthropocene by Shawna Ross £100.” “Reading time by specialised counsel of 326 pages of post-doctoral text £32,600.” Of course, they could save fifty quid by using the copy Dr Mills showed me at Hebden Bridge. They will find my thumb-print on page 68 where I had to point out the 1989 bog burst. Pinsent Masons must keep in mind that Ross, 2020 was Dr Mills’ own reference and we know for certain that he did not read it, so Pinsent Masons better had. There will be a test.

records.title: Our Power
records.bodyText:
An Scottish Trades Union Congress (STUC) investigation reveals Scotland is missing out on almost *£9 BILLION* from wind turbines on our own hills and seas. Their estimates say that money could fund 10,000 to 14,000 nurses for 20 years.
Instead, £500M of Scottish public money is subsidising private firms, while:
-90% of onshore wind profits are paid straight to corporate shareholders.
-Over 75% of ScotWind capacity is owned overseas by global asset managers like BlackRock and Vanguard, and oil giants Shell and BP.
-Wind creates just ONE job per £1M turnover, compared to 14 in oil and gas.
-Offshore workers transitioning face a 40% wage cut, while turbine parts ship in from China.
 European governments and multinational corporations take our wealth, leaving Scottish communities with crumbs.
Is this fair to Scotland? Drop your thoughts below.
